doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Do students today experience music as profoundly? Technology and attention
summary: Piltzecker thinks it is harder for students now, and discusses Harari and the encroachment of technology on humanity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And I’m wondering, you’re an educator now also. Do you think it’s harder for students these days to be profoundly affected the way you were because there’s so much out there and they have access to almost everything? Does it affect them the way it affected us?

Well it’s a great question, and a profound question because it relates to every aspect of our contemporary culture world wide today. I mean and there are many people that have addressed this: attention span difficulties, you know you can get into anything on a surface level in an instant by just a couple of clicks. And so yes, the answer is I think, unfortunately I do think it’s harder. Yet it’s still happening, it still happens, and there’s a sense of humanity that we all want to hold on to you know. I still believe, I believe in it. I haven’t thrown in the towel in terms of being resigned to technology or to a lifestyle which is technology driven, although that’s what it is, that’s where our life is going. And in reading some other material, I’ve been reading Yuval Harari is this really interesting © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

author who’s getting some attention these days. He wrote a book called Sapiens and followed up with a book called Homo Deus and he talks about the synthesis of technology and biology. And it’s really frightening where it goes. And it does relate to your question because it’s harder and harder to hold on to that sense of what jazz and music represents about our species and our humanity you know, as technology encroaches. And so there are things, you know implants — I don’t mean to get too off the subject here but what they’re doing now is experiments with rats where they implant the electrodes that clip and will dispense serotonin from their brain to another part of their brain. So now you have a control panel, as if you were flying a drone, and the rat’s in the cage, and you say, “Right turn,” “Left turn,” “Climb the stairs” and you push those buttons and that’s exactly what the rat does. So that’s a very frightening prospect. It’s a little bit of a diversion from your question but I still think maybe tangentially related. Because, yet, it’s a little hard for us to have this overwhelming aesthetic experience today. And I sort of feel protective of that experience and I’m hopeful that we will come out the other side and find some meeting ground, this technology evolves in the next fifty years that, the synthesis of man and machine is still of man. So I took your question out, sorry.
